paragraphs.notes: B06-01 ‘a high beach of shingle’ → ‘a high beach of pebbles’: a real barrier for the edition's American-English readers, for whom ‘shingle’ is a roofing tile or signboard; the beach sense is chiefly British. ‘pebbles’ is Homer's λάιγγας (6.94–95) and plain on both sides of the Atlantic. It is not a regionalism (unlike ‘checkers’ for ‘draughts’, which the Glossary refuses). This is Butler's only ‘shingle’, and his paragraph has no ‘pebble’, so there is no collision. Not merely a rewording: the BEFORE does not picture correctly for the target reader.

B06-02 ‘for he was in great want’ → ‘for he was in great need’: a listed dead sense, plus a decorum hazard. With a naked man approaching young women, ‘want’ can be read as desire. Verified precedent: the edition already renders Butler's identical phrase ‘I am in great want’ (14 ¶8, Odysseus as a beggar) as ‘I am in great need’, so this brings the two into line. Homer has χρειὼ γὰρ ἵκανε (6.136). The living idioms are kept, verified in the AFTER: 5 ¶30 ‘for want of a foothold’ and 6 ¶14 ‘you shall not want for clothes’. Butler's paragraph has no ‘need’, so there is no collision.

B06-03 ‘in the middle of it, paved with large stones’ → ‘in the middle of it, and paved with large stones’: restores Butler's own ‘and’ (D29), which makes ‘paved’ a second attribute of the marketplace. In Homer 6.266–267 the agora is paved. This removes the reported guess about which noun is paved. A with-absolute parse, in which the temple is paved, is still grammatically possible but is Butler's own structure and pragmatically unlikely, so the problem is fixed and nothing new is introduced. No other word moves. The quotation structure is unchanged: the speech continues into ¶21, so there is no closing quote, as in Butler.
